r: Introduction to Architecture develops appreciation for architectural culture, complexity, and aesthetics, guiding students toward a specialized area of interest — an informational, interpretive course, not embodied studio practice. The applied tasks map to O*NET's Getting Information, Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others, and Thinking Creatively: reading, contextualizing, and writing about the built environment. Task-exposure research classifies writing and explanatory work as strongly positively associated with exposure, and observed-usage data shows office and writing tasks are prominent in AI use, so the content-delivery and analytical-writing core is already substantially AI-competent. The one restraint is a modest foundational role: the catalog frames the course as a substrate students pursue through affiliated courses. But unlike the surveyed appreciation courses elsewhere in the catalog, it carries no GT-Pathways transfer designation or licensure mandate to lock it in. At 24 months the instrumental need is partly eroded — enough for Medium.

By 2031, AI systems will fluently generate architectural criticism, historical contextualization, and the explanatory prose at the center of an appreciation course, and can tutor a student toward a specialized interest interactively. Real-deliverable evaluations (GDPval) show models approaching expert parity on document-style occupational outputs, and professional-writing RCTs report roughly 40% time savings with quality gains — precisely the tasks this course exercises. Absent any transfer mandate or accreditation lock, little institutional friction slows that erosion; the residual value is the student's own cultivated critical and aesthetic literacy, which AI supplies to the learner only weakly. The binding consideration is the thin foundational role, which no longer caps exposure beyond the near term. The instrumental case for taking the course to acquire architectural appreciation weakens materially, supporting High, though how such courses are redesigned around AI remains genuinely uncertain.

A decade out, an AI interlocutor can deliver, contextualize, and critique architectural culture on demand, and the pure information-and-appreciation rationale is substantially eroded. The honest uncertainty is pedagogical rather than technical: whether an introductory appreciation course persists as a discussion-and-judgment seminar or is absorbed into AI-mediated self-study. Task-exposure research is consistent that explanatory writing sits at the exposed end of the frontier, and diffusion data (Census BTOS, adoption still uneven) is the main reason to hedge the timeline rather than the capability. Without a licensure gate, GT-Pathways designation, or strong prerequisite dependency to hold it structurally in place, nothing in this course's institutional context resists substitution the way accredited or foundational courses do. The rating holds High; the caveat is that appreciation courses may survive as forums for cultivating human judgment even where AI performs the informational work.
ARCH 2001.d: In this course, students will recognize the complexity and beauty of architecture, and develop a specialized area of interest within the field of architecture. The course provides a foundation in the culture of architecture, which students will pursue through affiliated courses on the subject.

r: Architectural Design-Studio 1 centers on a practical residential building design carried from concept through finished plan and documentation — a creative, synthesis-heavy studio, not a purely digital drafting exercise. The applied tasks map to O*NET's Thinking Creatively, Designing, and Drafting, Laying Out, and Specifying Technical Devices: spatial reasoning, iterative judgment, and code-conscious problem framing. Task-exposure research finds critical-thinking-intensive design work less exposed than routine writing, and the studio's in-person desk-crit culture and physical model-making are not activities generative tools perform for the learner. Generative floor-plan and rendering tools exist but are not competently deployed for buildable, client-responsive residential design at professional quality. No licensure or accreditation lock is retrieved for this program, so the protection is the design-judgment competence itself and the studio's partly embodied character. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop residential design judgment is largely intact, supporting Low.

By 2031, generative design tools will more capably produce candidate residential layouts, massings, and construction-document drafts, and small-scale dwelling design — comparatively templatable — is among the more automatable architectural tasks. The GitHub Copilot and professional-writing RCTs illustrate the pattern: large uplift on well-specified generative work, skewed toward lower-skill execution. Yet the jagged-frontier evidence is directly relevant — AI-generated designs of uneven, sometimes confidently wrong quality require a designer who can judge spatial resolution, code compliance, and constructability, and that verification competence is what the studio builds. With no institutional lock, the rating rises to Medium as execution automates, but the design-judgment core resists full substitution. The instrumental case shifts from producing drawings toward directing and critically evaluating AI-generated design options rather than disappearing.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating competent residential design options and much of the documentation this course teaches students to produce. The execution rationale erodes substantially, and small-scale dwelling design is more exposed than complex urban work. But the studio's purpose — cultivating spatial judgment and the capacity to specify, refine, and verify a buildable design — remains a human competence, and capability-trend data (fast task-horizon growth) is tempered by uneven real-world diffusion in the fragmented building sector, so timing is uncertain. Without a NAAB-style accreditation gate or foundational lock beyond feeding upper studios, little institutional friction holds the course in place; the residual is the judgment premium. The rating settles at Medium rather than High: even under aggressive automation, designing and verifying architecture is where the trained human is trusted to direct the tools, not simply replaced by them.
ARCH 2002.d: In this course, students will focus on a practical, residential building design. The small-scale dwelling design will include the overall planning process from creating a basic building concept to its finished plan and documentation.

r: Building Structures teaches structural components and details plus architectural modeling and Building Information Modeling (BIM), emphasizing cross-disciplinary collaboration in the building industry. The applied tasks map to O*NET's Analyzing Data or Information, Drafting, Laying Out, and Specifying Technical Devices, and Interacting With Computers — structural computation and digital modeling that are highly exposed, since observed-usage data shows computer-and-mathematical work is the single largest AI-use category. But the binding constraint is verification burden: a structural error is potentially catastrophic and its failure non-obvious, so oversight strictly requires a human who holds this knowledge, and the jagged-frontier caution about mis-calibrated trust applies acutely to load-bearing design. That dampener, plus the course's foundational role as structural literacy for downstream building design, holds the near-term rating at Low even though BIM automation and structural solvers are already capable and deployed.

By 2031, AI will more fluently perform structural analysis, generate and coordinate BIM models, and automate clash detection and documentation, deepening exposure of the course's computational tasks. Yet structural safety keeps a knowledgeable human necessary: verifying that an AI-generated structural scheme is sound, code-compliant, and constructable is exactly the adversarial, high-error-cost condition that sustains verification burden. The foundational role — this course scaffolds the structural reasoning later building-design work depends on — caps erosion further. Real-deliverable benchmarks (GDPval) show models still below expert parity on complex technical outputs, reinforcing that oversight, not replacement, is the near-term trajectory. The rating rises to Medium: analytical and modeling execution automates, but the structural-verification competence and the course's substrate role keep it instrumentally required rather than optional.

A decade out, AI-assisted structural design and BIM automation will handle most routine analysis and coordination, and the compute-and-model execution this course teaches is largely absorbed. But the human capacity to verify that an automated structural solution is safe — where errors carry real-world physical consequences — remains load-bearing, and structural literacy continues to scaffold building design. Capability trends point up sharply, yet uneven diffusion across the fragmented building industry, with adoption lagging capability, is a genuine reason to hedge. Without a retrieved ABET or licensure mandate for this program, the protection is verification burden and foundational role rather than institutional lock. The rating holds Medium: the profession reorganizes around AI structural tools, but competence to catch a dangerous, non-obvious structural error stays necessary, keeping the course instrumentally valuable through 2036.
ARCH 2003.d: In this course students learn building structural components and details and architectural modeling through integrated class projects. The students are also introduced to Building Information Modeling (BIM) and to the importance of collaboration between related fields in the building industry.

r: Architectural Interior Design explores interior design as both integral to complex architecture and independent, extending into object design — a creative studio in spatial composition, materials, and human-scale experience. The applied tasks map to O*NET's Thinking Creatively, Designing, and Drafting, Laying Out, and Specifying Technical Devices: developing interior concepts and resolving them into specified, buildable schemes. Generative image tools readily produce interior renderings and moodboards, creating real conceptual tension, but the studio competence is design judgment — spatial, ergonomic, and material reasoning — which those tools do not perform for the learner. Task-exposure research places critical-thinking-intensive design below routine writing on the exposure gradient. With no licensure or accreditation lock retrieved for this program, the protection is the judgment competence and the studio's partly in-person, model-based character. At 24 months the instrumental need to develop interior and object design judgment is largely intact, supporting Low.

By 2031, generative tools will produce interior schemes, material palettes, and object concepts with growing facility, and rendering-heavy tasks — where observed usage already shows strong creative-image adoption — are meaningfully exposed. Productivity RCTs show large uplift on well-specified generative work, skewed toward lower-skill execution. But interior design integrates ergonomics, circulation, code, and client experience into a resolved whole, and the jagged-frontier evidence warns that AI-generated interiors of uneven quality require a designer who can judge what actually works spatially and materially. Absent an institutional lock, the rating rises to Medium as concept-generation automates, while the synthesis-and-judgment core resists full substitution. The instrumental case shifts toward directing and critically curating AI-generated design options, and toward the object-design and buildable-specification work that remains harder to automate end-to-end.

A decade out, AI will generate sophisticated interior and object concepts and much specification on demand, substantially eroding the execution rationale. Yet the studio's aim — cultivating the judgment to resolve interiors that are functional, code-conscious, and experientially coherent, and to verify AI proposals against real spatial constraints — remains a human competence. Capability trends run fast, but uneven diffusion and the client-specific, context-laden nature of interior work are reasons to hedge the timeline. With no retrieved accreditation gate or strong downstream-prerequisite dependency, the course lacks institutional lock; its durability rests on the design-judgment premium. The rating settles at Medium rather than High: even as generation becomes routine, specifying and validating a buildable interior is where the trained human is trusted to direct the tools rather than be displaced by them through 2036.
ARCH 3001.d: In this course, students will focus on the dual nature of interior design and architecture. One part will reveal how interior design is an integral part of complex architecture; the other part will show how interior design is independent. The main goal is for students to gain experience in interior design and the exciting world of object design.

r: Architectural Design-Studio 2 addresses complex architectural issues at the scale of public building and urban design, connecting projects to urbanism, planning history, and large-scale development through case studies from precedent to implementation. The applied tasks map to O*NET's Thinking Creatively, Developing Objectives and Strategies, and Making Decisions and Solving Problems — synthesizing site, program, stakeholders, and context into resolved urban proposals. This is among the least automatable design work: task-exposure research finds complex critical-thinking and judgment strongly negatively associated with exposure, and urban design's multi-stakeholder, context-dependent character resists generative substitution more than templatable residential work. No licensure or accreditation lock is retrieved, but the judgment competence and studio process are the protection. At 24 months, generative tools can produce massing options or renderings but not competently resolve a complex urban-development scheme, so the instrumental need is intact — Low.

By 2031, generative and analytical tools will more capably support urban-scale exploration — massing studies, precedent synthesis, and visualization — augmenting rather than replacing the designer. Real-deliverable benchmarks (GDPval) show models still short of expert parity on complex, multi-constraint outputs, and urban design layers political, regulatory, and stakeholder considerations that raise the verification burden on any AI-proposed scheme. The jagged-frontier evidence — sharp accuracy drops when users over-trust AI outside its competence — is acute where a plausible but unworkable urban proposal carries public consequences. Absent an institutional lock, the rating stays Low: the complexity and judgment density of urban design keep the studio competence instrumentally necessary across this horizon, even as tools absorb more of the representational and analytical support work rather than the core synthesis.

A decade out, AI will contribute substantially to urban analysis, scenario generation, and visualization, and the representational tasks this studio teaches are largely automatable; the base automatability finally ticks up as generative design encroaches on adjacent work. But resolving a complex public-building or urban-development scheme — integrating contested stakeholder interests, regulation, and long-horizon implementation — is judgment-dense work that capability trends have not clearly shown AI performing autonomously, and uneven real-world diffusion in planning contexts is a further reason to hedge. With no retrieved accreditation or licensure gate, the protection is the difficulty and consequence of the work itself. The rating moves to Medium at 2036: more of the studio's execution automates, but the human capacity to synthesize and verify complex urban design remains instrumentally valuable, keeping the course from full substitution.
ARCH 3002.d: This course provides a knowledge base in the theory and practice of architecture and urban design, focusing on complex architectural issues. Students will explore the relationship of public building design and urbanism. Students will gain insight into the connections between architectural projects and urban design, and overview urban planning history from its beginnings to the present. Students learn to create large-scale, urban-development projects through case studies that demonstrate design precedents, to procedure, to implementation.

r: Digital Presentations in Architecture teaches traditional and contemporary presentation techniques across media platforms, aiming to let students self-manage their professional life and communicate work creatively. The applied tasks map to O*NET's Thinking Creatively, Interacting With Computers, Communicating With Persons Outside the Organization, and Documenting/Recording Information — assembling renderings, portfolios, boards, and digital media. These are among the most exposed activities in the evidence base: observed-usage data shows writing, office, and computer tasks dominate AI use, and image and layout generation is directly targeted by current tools. Presentation output is low-stakes and easily checked, so verification imposes little brake, and no licensure or accreditation lock is retrieved. Even at 24 months, AI competently drafts, renders, and formats much presentation media, so the instrumental need to take a dedicated course to produce it is already partly eroded — Medium.

By 2031, generative tools will fluently produce architectural renderings, animated walkthroughs, portfolio layouts, and platform-tailored media, automating most of the production this course teaches. Professional-writing and design-productivity RCTs report large time savings and quality gains on exactly this kind of well-specified creative-communication work, and observed usage shows strong adoption of creative-image and document tasks. There is no verification brake — presentation errors are low-cost and obvious — and no institutional lock to hold the course in place. The residual competence is curatorial and rhetorical judgment: deciding what to present and how to persuade, which AI supports but does not own. The rating rises to High: the instrumental case for a course in producing digital presentation media weakens sharply as generation becomes push-button, though the self-management-of-a-professional-life aim retains some human-judgment content.

A decade out, producing polished architectural presentation media — renderings, films, interactive portfolios — is effectively automated, and the production rationale for this course is largely gone. Capability trends point strongly that way, and the low-stakes, fully digital nature of the work removes the verification and embodiment brakes that protect other architecture courses. The honest hedge is diffusion and pedagogy rather than capability: uneven adoption, and the possibility that such a course refocuses on rhetorical strategy and self-presentation judgment, which are less automatable than media production. But with no licensure gate, transfer mandate, or foundational dependency, nothing institutional resists substitution. The rating holds High: by 2036 the instrumental need to learn to produce digital presentations, as distinct from cultivating communication judgment, is substantially displaced by competent generative tooling.
ARCH 3003.d: The course introduces students to traditional and contemporary presentation techniques that could be applied to the architecture profession. The goal of the course is to enable students to self-manage their professional life and creatively use different media platforms. Art
